options.a: Help the client build awareness and small actions
options.b: Calculate exact macros and hand over a full meal plan
options.c: Start a 30-day elimination diet to find food triggers
options.d: Set a weekly weight-loss target to build urgency

distractorExplanations.b: PN coaching starts with awareness and small actions; a full macro meal plan on day one overloads a new client.
distractorExplanations.c: Elimination diets are a clinical tool, not a first coaching step; PN begins with awareness and one small action.
distractorExplanations.d: Imposed outcome targets are not PN's first step; PN focuses first on behaviors the client controls.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: Coaching before a meal plan dump. This item asks: “A PN partner's first job is usually to:”. The matching answer is: Help the client build awareness and small actions, not write a 12-week contest diet on day one. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official Precision Nutrition paper. PN does not write a 12-week contest diet on day one; it starts with awareness and one small action.

options.a: Restart the program from week one
options.b: Get curious about what happened
options.c: Add extra cardio to offset it
options.d: Tighten their weekend calorie target

distractorExplanations.a: Restarting from scratch treats one weekend as total failure; PN gets curious and adjusts from where the client is.
distractorExplanations.c: Compensatory exercise frames food as something to pay off and reinforces a binge-punish cycle.
distractorExplanations.d: Tightening restriction after a lapse often drives the next lapse; first understand what happened.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: Data, not drama. This item asks: “If a client says they 'failed' the weekend, you:”. The matching answer is: Get curious about what happened — skip the shame lecture. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official Precision Nutrition paper. Skip the shame lecture; curiosity shows what got in the way and what to adjust.

options.a: Keep the plan unchanged until the 12-week reassessment
options.b: Choose the next action from the client's original intake goals
options.c: Change the next action based on what the client actually did
options.d: Change the plan whenever scale weight stalls for two days

distractorExplanations.a: Outcome-based coaching adjusts each step from fresh data; waiting 12 weeks ignores what the client is doing now.
distractorExplanations.b: Intake goals set direction, but outcome-based decisions use what actually happened since, not starting assumptions.
distractorExplanations.d: Two days of scale noise is not a meaningful outcome; decisions weigh behaviors, feelings, and performance over time.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: Measure, then adjust. This item asks: “Outcome-based decision making means:”. The matching answer is: Change the next action based on what the client actually did and how they feel/perform. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official Precision Nutrition paper. Outcome-based decisions also weigh how the client feels and performs, not just the plan on paper.

options.a: A full meal plan to follow at every meal
options.b: Three new habits at once to build momentum
options.c: Daily calorie tracking in an app
options.d: One clear, small, repeatable behavior

distractorExplanations.a: A full meal plan is many behaviors at once; PN starts with one small, repeatable behavior.
distractorExplanations.b: Stacking several new habits at once lowers adherence; PN introduces one habit at a time.
distractorExplanations.c: Full calorie tracking is a high-effort skill; it is not usually the first habit for a new client.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: Small enough to repeat. This item asks: “A good first habit is often:”. The matching answer is: One clear, small, repeatable behavior (protein at breakfast, a walk after lunch). Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official Precision Nutrition paper. Examples: protein at breakfast or a walk after lunch.

options.a: Pick the one they can do on a bad day
options.b: Pick the one with the biggest fat-loss impact
options.c: Pick the one the coach thinks matters most
options.d: Run both and see which one sticks

distractorExplanations.b: The highest-impact habit is useless if it fails under stress; PN picks what the client can do on a bad day.
distractorExplanations.c: Coach priority ignores client confidence; PN chooses the habit the client can do even on a bad day.
distractorExplanations.d: Running competing habits at once dilutes effort; PN chooses the one the client can sustain on a bad day.

options.a: Use a strict meal plan that removes daily food choices
options.b: Use plate methods, photos, or one-item checklists
options.c: Use weekly weigh-ins as the only progress measure
options.d: Wait to start coaching until they agree to log

distractorExplanations.a: A rigid meal plan is a bigger demand than tracking for most clients; PN offers lighter tools like plate methods or photos.
distractorExplanations.c: Scale weight alone misses behaviors and other outcomes; PN uses plate methods, photos, or checklists to track habits.
distractorExplanations.d: Refusing to coach until logging begins ignores readiness; PN meets clients with lower-effort tracking tools.

options.a: Low motivation — raise the stakes with deadlines
options.b: A sign the plan is too easy — add challenge
options.c: Ambivalence — use better questions, not a lecture
options.d: Noncompliance — restate the rules more clearly

distractorExplanations.a: Pressure and deadlines escalate resistance; PN reads resistance as ambivalence and explores it with questions.
distractorExplanations.b: Resistance usually signals the plan is too much or not wanted; adding challenge increases it.
distractorExplanations.d: Treating resistance as rule-breaking leads to lecturing; motivational interviewing explores ambivalence instead.

options.a: Required at intake to measure progress
options.b: Shareable once the client signs up
options.c: Taken by the coach during each session
options.d: Optional, private, and consented

distractorExplanations.a: Photos can help but must be optional; making them a condition of coaching ignores consent and body-image risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Signing up is not consent to share images; photos stay private unless the client gives specific permission.
distractorExplanations.c: Coach-taken photos at every session remove client control; photos are optional and client-consented.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: Body photos are sensitive. This item asks: “A progress photo request should be:”. The matching answer is: Optional, private, and consented — never a public before/after without permission. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official Precision Nutrition paper. Never post a public before/after without explicit permission.

options.a: Reach out with a short, kind re-onboard
options.b: Pause their account until they reply
options.c: Send a reminder of the commitment they signed
options.d: Assign extra habits to catch up on missed work

distractorExplanations.b: Pausing without contact is effectively ghosting; PN reaches out with a short, kind re-onboard.
distractorExplanations.c: Pointing to their signed commitment adds guilt; a kind, brief re-onboard rebuilds engagement better.
distractorExplanations.d: Adding habits after a lapse increases load when the client is already struggling; shrink the ask instead.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: Re-engagement is the skill. This item asks: “If they miss three check-ins, you:”. The matching answer is: Reach out with a short, kind re-onboard — do not ghost or scold. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official Precision Nutrition paper. Do not ghost or scold; make the way back easy.

options.a: A strict week followed by a free weekend
options.b: A perfect day repeated twice a week
options.c: An 80–90% week they can repeat
options.d: A fresh Monday restart each week

distractorExplanations.a: Strict-then-free cycles mimic restrict-binge patterns; repeatable 80–90% consistency beats them.
distractorExplanations.b: Isolated perfect days are still not a repeatable pattern; PN values a sustainable 80–90% week.
distractorExplanations.d: Weekly restarts reflect all-or-nothing thinking; consistent 80–90% weeks outperform repeated fresh starts.

options.a: You are lecturing, not coaching
options.b: The client needs more information first
options.c: You are building rapport fast
options.d: The session is running efficiently

distractorExplanations.b: Information overload is the problem; when the coach dominates the talk, the client does less thinking and owning.
distractorExplanations.c: Rapport grows from listening; a coach-dominated session usually means lecturing, not connection.
distractorExplanations.d: Efficiency is not the goal if the client is passive; talking more than the client usually means lecturing.

options.a: A sign the client lacks motivation
options.b: An environment problem to problem-solve
options.c: A relationship issue outside nutrition coaching
options.d: A willpower test the client must pass

distractorExplanations.a: Partner sabotage is an environmental barrier, not a motivation deficit; blaming the client ignores the real fix.
distractorExplanations.c: The household food environment is squarely in coaching scope; the coach problem-solves it rather than declaring it off-limits.
distractorExplanations.d: Relying on willpower against a hostile environment fails; PN redesigns the environment instead.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-c.explanation: Environment eats willpower. This item asks: “A client's partner sabotaging dinners is:”. The matching answer is: An environment problem to problem-solve, not a moral failing. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official Precision Nutrition paper. It is not a moral failing of the client; change the setup around dinners.

options.a: The official PN Level 1 final exam in timed form
options.b: A licensed dietetics practice exam from CDR
options.c: Independent practice — not the official PN L1 exam
options.d: A NASM CPT practice form reused for nutrition

distractorExplanations.a: This is an independent practice mock; it is not the official Precision Nutrition Level 1 exam.
distractorExplanations.b: CDR administers the RD exam; PN Level 1 is a coaching certification, not a dietetics license exam.
distractorExplanations.d: NASM CPT is a separate personal trainer certification; this mock targets PN Level 1 content.

options.a: Provide the main fuel for intense training
options.b: Raise metabolism enough to replace a deficit
options.c: Supply essential fatty acids for hormones
options.d: Support satiety and muscle in a deficit

distractorExplanations.a: Carbohydrate is the primary fuel for high-intensity training; protein's role is satiety and muscle retention.
distractorExplanations.b: Protein's higher thermic effect is small; it cannot replace a calorie deficit for fat loss.
distractorExplanations.c: Essential fatty acids come from dietary fat, not protein; protein supports satiety and lean mass.

options.a: Most fat loss over time
options.b: Most first-week scale drops
options.c: Fat loss only with low carbs
options.d: Daily weight changes

distractorExplanations.b: First-week scale drops are mostly glycogen and water, not fat; the deficit explains fat loss over time.
distractorExplanations.c: Fat loss follows a calorie deficit whether carbs are low or high; low-carb is one way to create it.
distractorExplanations.d: Daily weight swings reflect water, sodium, and gut content; a deficit explains the longer-term fat-loss trend.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: Energy balance still exists. This item asks: “A calorie deficit explains:”. The matching answer is: Most fat loss over time, not a spice detox. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official Precision Nutrition paper. Fat loss comes from a sustained energy deficit, not a spice detox.

options.a: Absorbing water-soluble vitamins such as C and B12
options.b: Hormones, fat-soluble vitamins, and food enjoyment
options.c: Building muscle tissue as the main structural macro
options.d: Fueling high-intensity sprints as the main energy source

distractorExplanations.a: Fat aids absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), not water-soluble ones like vitamin C and B vitamins.
distractorExplanations.c: Protein, not fat, is the main structural macronutrient for building muscle tissue.
distractorExplanations.d: High-intensity efforts rely mainly on carbohydrate (glycogen); fat fuels lower-intensity work.

options.a: A nonessential macro best cut to lose fat
options.b: The main driver of fat gain via insulin
options.c: A useful fuel, especially around training
options.d: Fuel that should be eaten mainly in the morning

distractorExplanations.a: Cutting carbs is not required for fat loss; a calorie deficit is, whatever the macro split.
distractorExplanations.b: The carbohydrate-insulin model is not supported as the main cause of fat gain; total energy balance is.
distractorExplanations.d: Carb timing by time of day has little effect for most clients; around training is the more useful timing.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: PN is not keto-or-bust. This item asks: “Carbohydrate is:”. The matching answer is: A useful fuel, especially around training — not a toxin. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official Precision Nutrition paper. Carbohydrate is not a toxin; it fuels training and fits most eating patterns.

options.a: Muscle protein synthesis
options.b: Fat-soluble vitamin uptake
options.c: Rapid glycogen refilling
options.d: Satiety and GI regularity

distractorExplanations.a: Muscle protein synthesis depends on protein intake and training, not fiber.
distractorExplanations.b: Fat-soluble vitamin absorption needs dietary fat; fiber helps satiety and regularity.
distractorExplanations.c: Rapid glycogen refilling needs fast-digesting carbs; fiber slows digestion and absorption.

options.a: Intolerance, habit, or something medical
options.b: Confirmed by removing the food for one week
options.c: A gluten allergy that a coach can rule in
options.d: Verified with an at-home IgG food panel

distractorExplanations.b: A short self-elimination cannot confirm an IgE allergy; diagnosis needs medical testing.
distractorExplanations.c: Bloating is not a gluten allergy diagnosis, and coaches cannot diagnose celiac disease or allergy.
distractorExplanations.d: IgG panels are not validated for diagnosing food allergy or intolerance; refer to a medical provider.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: Stay in scope. This item asks: “A food 'allergy' the client self-diagnosed from bloating may be:”. The matching answer is: Intolerance, habit, or something medical — you do not confirm IgE. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official Precision Nutrition paper. A coach does not confirm an IgE allergy; suspected allergy goes to a medical provider for testing.

options.a: A carbohydrate source counted as sugar
options.b: Energy-dense and often a habit trigger
options.c: Helpful for muscle recovery after training
options.d: Calorie-free when mixed with diet soda

distractorExplanations.a: Alcohol is its own energy source (about 7 kcal/g), not a carbohydrate counted as sugar.
distractorExplanations.c: Alcohol impairs muscle protein synthesis and sleep, so it hinders recovery rather than helping.
distractorExplanations.d: The alcohol itself supplies about 7 kcal per gram regardless of a diet mixer.

options.a: A fixed gallon of water daily for every client
options.b: Drinking only when thirst becomes strong
options.c: Regular fluids; pale-yellow urine as a crude check
options.d: Perfectly clear urine as the daily target

distractorExplanations.a: Fluid needs vary by body size, climate, and activity; a fixed gallon for everyone is a myth.
distractorExplanations.b: Strong thirst lags behind need, especially during exercise; regular fluid intake is the basic advice.
distractorExplanations.d: Clear urine can signal overdrinking; pale yellow is the crude check, not perfectly clear.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: Water is a habit. This item asks: “Hydration advice that is safe and basic is:”. The matching answer is: Regular fluids; pale-yellow urine as a crude check — not gallon-or-die. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official Precision Nutrition paper. Avoid gallon-or-die rules; fluid needs vary by person and conditions.

options.a: A multivitamin
options.b: Fortified cereals alone
options.c: Large-dose single vitamins
options.d: A varied diet first

distractorExplanations.a: A multivitamin can fill specific gaps, but a varied diet comes first for micronutrients.
distractorExplanations.b: Fortified foods add some nutrients but miss fiber and phytonutrients; variety covers more.
distractorExplanations.c: High single-nutrient doses risk imbalance or toxicity; food variety is the first-line approach.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: Food first. This item asks: “Micronutrients are best covered by:”. The matching answer is: A varied diet first, not 20 random pills you sell. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official Precision Nutrition paper. Food variety comes before supplements; do not push 20 random pills you sell.

options.a: Glycogen, sodium, GI content
options.b: Mostly body fat from one meal
options.c: Muscle tissue lost overnight
options.d: Metabolic slowdown from the diet

distractorExplanations.b: Gaining 4 lb of fat overnight would need about 14,000 extra kcal; the change is water and gut content.
distractorExplanations.c: Muscle cannot be lost in that amount overnight; rapid swings are glycogen, water, sodium, and gut content.
distractorExplanations.d: Adaptive thermogenesis is slow and small; it cannot cause a 4 lb overnight change.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: Teach water weight. This item asks: “A sudden 4 lb overnight change is usually:”. The matching answer is: Glycogen, sodium, GI content — not 4 lb of fat. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official Precision Nutrition paper. It is not 4 lb of fat; water shifts and gut content explain overnight swings.

options.a: The same as TDEE
options.b: Calories at rest
options.c: Calories burned in exercise
options.d: Calories used to digest food

distractorExplanations.c: Calories burned during exercise are exercise activity thermogenesis, one part of TDEE, not RMR.
distractorExplanations.d: Energy used to digest food is the thermic effect of food, not resting metabolic rate.
distractorExplanations.a: “The same as TDEE” does not answer “RMR is:”. The matching answer is: Calories at rest — not a number you invent from an Instagram calculator as medical truth.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: Estimates are estimates. This item asks: “RMR is:”. The matching answer is: Calories at rest — not a number you invent from an Instagram calculator as medical truth. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official Precision Nutrition paper. Treat calculator estimates as estimates, not as a number you invent from an Instagram calculator as medical truth.

options.a: A small part of expenditure, higher for fat
options.b: The largest part of daily energy expenditure
options.c: A small part of expenditure, higher for protein
options.d: A large part of expenditure, highest for carbohydrate

distractorExplanations.a: Fat has the lowest thermic effect (about 0–3%); protein has the highest (about 20–30%).
distractorExplanations.b: RMR is the largest component of TDEE; TEF is only about 10%.
distractorExplanations.d: TEF is about 10% of expenditure, and protein, not carbohydrate, has the highest thermic effect.

options.a: Needs more cardio to boost energy levels
options.b: Should add caffeine to push through
options.c: Is adapting and should stay the course
options.d: May need more food or medical review

distractorExplanations.a: Adding cardio to an exhausted, under-fueled client deepens the energy deficit.
distractorExplanations.b: Stimulants mask fatigue without fixing low energy availability; the client may need more food or medical review.
distractorExplanations.c: Persistent exhaustion on a very low-calorie diet is a warning sign, not normal adaptation to push through.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: Symptoms are data. This item asks: “A client on a very low-calorie diet who is exhausted:”. The matching answer is: May need more food or medical review — not another cut. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official Precision Nutrition paper. Another cut is the wrong move when an under-fueled client is exhausted.

options.a: A well-studied supplement you still do not prescribe
options.b: An anabolic steroid that is banned in competitive sport
options.c: Proven harmful to kidneys in healthy adults
options.d: Useful only for endurance athletes

distractorExplanations.b: Creatine is a legal, non-hormonal compound, not an anabolic steroid, and it is not banned by WADA.
distractorExplanations.c: Research in healthy people shows no kidney harm at standard doses; existing kidney disease is a referral issue.
distractorExplanations.d: Creatine mainly benefits short, high-intensity efforts and strength, not endurance specifically.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: Stay educational, not a pharmacy. This item asks: “Creatine monohydrate, if they ask, is:”. The matching answer is: A well-studied supplement you still do not prescribe as a drug. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official Precision Nutrition paper. Coaches can share evidence but do not prescribe it as a drug.

options.a: A visual split of calories into exact gram targets
options.b: A visual split of protein, produce, and smart carbs/fats
options.c: A rule to finish the whole plate before taking second helpings
options.d: A portion guide using hands for each macronutrient

distractorExplanations.a: Exact gram targets are macro counting; the plate method uses visual portions instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Finishing the plate is a clean-plate rule, not the plate method's visual split of food groups.
distractorExplanations.d: Using palms, fists, and thumbs is PN's hand-portion method, a related but different tool from the plate split.

options.a: Add several new habits in the same week
options.b: Pair a habit with a reward afterward
options.c: Attach a new action to an existing routine
options.d: Track habits together in one app

distractorExplanations.a: Adding many habits at once is overload; habit stacking links one new action to an existing routine.
distractorExplanations.b: Rewarding after a behavior is reinforcement; stacking anchors the new action to an existing routine.
distractorExplanations.d: Logging habits in one place is tracking, not stacking a new action onto an existing cue.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.explanation: Cue is already in the day. This item asks: “Habit stacking means:”. The matching answer is: Attach a new action to an existing routine (after coffee, walk). Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official Precision Nutrition paper. Example: after morning coffee, take a short walk.

options.a: Skipped until the next good day
options.b: The same size to keep standards high
options.c: Made up with a double dose tomorrow
options.d: Even smaller so the streak survives

distractorExplanations.a: Skipping breaks the pattern; a smaller bad-day version keeps the habit alive.
distractorExplanations.b: Holding the full version on a bad day invites failure; shrink it so consistency survives.
distractorExplanations.c: Doubling up later is compensatory thinking; the bad-day version is simply smaller and done today.

options.a: Protein food visible; candy off the counter
options.b: Willpower reminders posted on the fridge
options.c: A food log app with daily reminders
options.d: Keeping treats visible to practice restraint

distractorExplanations.b: Reminders rely on willpower; environment design changes what is visible and easy instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Tracking prompts are monitoring tools, not changes to the physical food environment.
distractorExplanations.d: Visible treats increase cue-driven eating; environment design makes the better choice easier, not temptation louder.

options.a: 'I will lose 20 pounds by summer' with a deadline
options.b: 'I'm someone who cooks on Sundays' plus a tiny proof
options.c: 'I have to stop eating junk' as a daily rule
options.d: 'I'm someone who cooks on Sundays' with no action yet

distractorExplanations.a: That is an outcome goal with a deadline, not an identity statement backed by proof.
distractorExplanations.c: A 'have to' rule is a restriction, not an identity; identity change is 'I'm someone who…' plus small proof.
distractorExplanations.d: Identity statements need small actions as proof; a label without evidence does not build the identity.

options.a: It burns most daily calories during rest
options.b: It matters mainly for muscle gain clients
options.c: It changes hunger, training, and adherence
options.d: It lets coaches screen for sleep apnea

distractorExplanations.a: Sleep burns little extra energy; its importance is its effect on hunger hormones, training, and adherence.
distractorExplanations.b: Sleep affects appetite, recovery, and adherence for every goal, not mainly muscle gain.
distractorExplanations.d: Screening for sleep apnea is medical; a coach refers suspected apnea rather than diagnosing it.

options.a: A willpower problem to push through
options.b: Fixed by a stricter calorie target
options.c: A sign of binge eating disorder
options.d: A skill gap, not a character flaw

distractorExplanations.a: Framing stress-eating as weak willpower ignores the missing coping skills PN teaches.
distractorExplanations.b: Tighter restriction adds stress and usually worsens stress-eating.
distractorExplanations.c: Occasional stress-eating is common and not an ED diagnosis; coaches do not diagnose, and refer if signs persist.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.explanation: Skills > labels. This item asks: “Stress-eating is often:”. The matching answer is: A skill gap (pause, protein, walk) not a character flaw. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official Precision Nutrition paper. Teach skills such as pausing, eating protein, or taking a walk.

options.a: What worked, what blocked, what's next one change
options.b: How many rules they broke and why it happened
options.c: Which three new habits to add next week
options.d: What their weight did and the new calorie target

distractorExplanations.b: Counting broken rules is a compliance audit that breeds shame; PN reviews what worked, what blocked, and one next change.
distractorExplanations.c: Adding several habits at once overloads the client; the review picks one next change.
distractorExplanations.d: Scale-plus-target reviews focus on outcomes; PN reviews behaviors, barriers, and one next change.

options.a: Skipping social meals until goal weight
options.b: A plan (protein first, one treat, leave when done)
options.c: Eating very little all day to bank calories for the event
options.d: Fasting the day after to make up for it

distractorExplanations.a: Avoidance is not sustainable; PN plans for social meals instead of removing them.
distractorExplanations.c: Banking calories often leads to overeating at the event; a simple plan works better.
distractorExplanations.d: Compensatory fasting reinforces restrict-binge cycles; PN plans ahead rather than punishing after.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.explanation: Life is the program. This item asks: “Social meals are handled by:”. The matching answer is: A plan (protein first, one treat, leave when done) not avoidance forever. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official Precision Nutrition paper. Planning beats avoiding social meals forever.

options.a: They are done once a month for less stress
options.b: They decide whether the week was a success
options.c: They are a data point among others
options.d: They follow a big meal to see the real number

distractorExplanations.a: Frequency is not the issue; weigh-ins help when read as one data point among others, not a verdict.
distractorExplanations.b: Using the scale as the week's verdict is exactly what PN avoids; it is one data point among several.
distractorExplanations.d: Weighing after a big meal shows food and water weight, not fat change; it misleads rather than informs.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.explanation: Context the number. This item asks: “Weigh-ins work better when:”. The matching answer is: They are a data point among others, not a daily verdict. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official Precision Nutrition paper. The scale is not a daily verdict; read it alongside behaviors, measurements, and how the client feels.

options.a: Proof the plan needs restarting
options.b: A reason to skip the next meal
options.c: Resolved with tomorrow's restart
options.d: Expected — resume the next meal

distractorExplanations.a: A single slip does not mean starting over; PN expects slips and resumes at the next meal.
distractorExplanations.b: Skipping the next meal to compensate starts a restrict-binge cycle; just resume normally.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiting for tomorrow turns one slip into a lost day; resume at the very next meal.

options.a: Get muted — design fewer, better cues
options.b: Build discipline through repetition
options.c: Raise adherence for most clients
options.d: Work best when sent at random times

distractorExplanations.b: Hourly nagging leads to notification fatigue and muting, not discipline.
distractorExplanations.c: Frequent nags cause alert fatigue; fewer, well-timed cues work better for adherence.
distractorExplanations.d: Random-timed cues are harder to anchor to routines; fewer cues tied to specific moments work better.

options.a: Burns enough calories to replace lifting
options.b: Helps glucose and consistency for many clients
options.c: Should be avoided because it slows digestion
options.d: Matters mainly for clients with diabetes

distractorExplanations.a: Light walking is low intensity and does not provide the strength stimulus of resistance training.
distractorExplanations.c: Gentle post-meal walking is well tolerated and blunts glucose spikes; it does not harmfully slow digestion.
distractorExplanations.d: Post-meal walks help glucose and consistency for many clients, not just those with diabetes.

options.a: A shopping list built from meals they cook
options.b: Reading labels for protein and fiber
options.c: A PDF of foods they will never cook
options.d: A simple weekly meal-prep routine

distractorExplanations.a: A list built from meals the client actually cooks is a grocery skill itself, not the thing it beats.
distractorExplanations.b: Label reading is part of grocery skills, so it is not what those skills replace.
distractorExplanations.d: Meal prep complements grocery skills; what they beat is a food list the client will never cook.

options.a: Strict weekday rules with weekends off-plan
options.b: A lower calorie target to offset eating out
options.c: Same meals as weekdays with no eating out
options.d: One planned meal out + default breakfast

distractorExplanations.a: Weekends fully off-plan create a 48-hour blackout that undoes the week; PN plans one meal out.
distractorExplanations.b: Pre-cutting calories for the weekend sets up overeating; structure with defaults works better.
distractorExplanations.c: Banning meals out is not sustainable; PN builds one planned meal out into the weekend.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.explanation: Plan the predictable chaos. This item asks: “Weekend structure might be:”. The matching answer is: One planned meal out + default breakfast, not a 48-hour blackout. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official Precision Nutrition paper. That structure avoids a 48-hour weekend blackout.

options.a: Discuss vegetable intake and meal timing
options.b: Diagnose disease or deprescribe medication
options.c: Ask about sleep and stress habits
